item.title: A welcome recovery milestone for Pope Leo after cancer surgery
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV was discharged from the hospital on Saturday after having surgery to remove a cancerous nodule in his lungs.

Why it matters: His discharge clears the way for his rigorous upcoming travel schedule and may alleviate fears of a leadership vacuum at the Vatican.

What they're saying: "In light of the blood tests and chest X-ray performed this morning, and following an assessment of his clinical condition, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge," The Holy See Press Office said in a Saturday statement attributed to Leo's doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora.

Catch up quick: The Vatican announced Leo would be having surgery to remove a nodule from his lung on Oct. 11, and later said the surgery removed the lower lobe of his right lung.

  • The Vatican confirmed the surgery was successful on Tuesday, and later said that Leo was walking around, eating normally, and that his blood tests and chest X-rays were normal.
  • Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer, per the Cancer Center, and if caught early, survival rates are very high.

Zoom out: His hospitalization and subsequent cancer diagnosis struck fear into Catholics across the world, who offered him prayers and well-wishes as he recovered.

  • For example, a group in Chicago, the first American Pontiff's hometown, created a care package for Leo featuring get-well cards and a Chicago White Sox blanket.
  • The Vatican has not yet said if any additional treatment is needed.

item.title: That Y2K feeling: Why today's economy resembles 2000
item.description:
It was an economy bursting at the seams: robust growth powered by a tech boom, low unemployment, elevated inflation and Fed rate hikes to try to cool things down.

The big picture: That was the situation in the year 2000, and it reminds us a great deal of the conditions in 2026.

  • The worrying part, however, is this: Then, as now, there were early warning signs that the technological boom powering the good times may not last forever.
  • And indeed, the cracks that appeared in the tech sector in 2000 would spill over into a broader bear market and mild recession in 2001.
  • We're not predicting that this time. History only rhymes; it doesn't repeat. But it is a historical episode worth weighing when thinking about the range of possibilities for how things may go in 2027 and beyond — particularly this week, as the debt markets funding the AI build-out have wobbled.

Flashback: While 2001 was a nasty year for the U.S. economy — a full-fledged tech bust exacerbated by the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks — the year before was pretty great by nearly every measure.

  • The unemployment rate reached a multi-decade low of 3.8% in April 2000 and closed the year at a mere 3.9%.
  • GDP rose 4.1% for the full year, powered by stunning rates of productivity growth.
  • It coincided, however, with high inflation, driven particularly by surging energy costs. The Consumer Price Index was up 3.4% over the course of the year.

Zoom in: Against that backdrop, the Alan Greenspan-led Fed felt compelled to try to cool things down, lest that inflation become more entrenched. The central bank increased rates three times that year, including a super-sized half-point in May.

  • But here's where the parallels to today get even more interesting: Greenspan's justification for rate hikes could be lifted from today's Fedspeak about the AI boom — or would be if today's central bankers shared his penchant for circumlocution.

What they're saying: The "profoundly beneficial forces driving the American economy to competitive excellence are also engendering a set of imbalances that, unless contained, threaten our continuing prosperity," Greenspan told Congress in February 2000.

  • "The problem is that the pickup in productivity tends to create even greater increases in aggregate demand than in potential aggregate supply," he said.
  • "This occurs principally because a rise in structural productivity growth has its counterpart in higher expectations for long-term corporate earnings."
  • "This, in turn, not only spurs business investment but also increases stock prices and the market value of assets held by households, creating additional purchasing power for which no additional goods or services have yet been produced."

Between the lines: He was talking about the productivity boom driven by the internet and related IT innovations of that era, but it is very much applicable to the AI boom today.

  • Yes, AI-fueled productivity could create a boost to the economy's supply potential in the future, with corresponding noninflationary growth and higher incomes.
  • But that's in the future. Right now, that potential is causing surging asset prices and rising demand for inputs to the build-out, pushing inflation higher.

Reality check: The stock market peaked in March 2000. By 2001, an all-out tech rout was underway, as much of the investment in fiber-optic cable and other internet infrastructure was ahead of its time.

  • That reversed the playing field for the Fed, as the wealth effects and an investment boom that appeared to be overheating the economy in 2000 instead dragged it down.
  • The Fed enacted a surprise half-point rate cut on Jan. 3, 2001, and would ultimately cut rates 11 times (!) in 2001.

Yes, but: Interestingly, while the tech bust hammered Americans' wealth, employment prospects and capital spending, the turn-of-the-century productivity gains continued throughout that recession and the ensuing jobless recovery.

The bottom line: Even if the AI boom drives the kinds of long-term productivity surges its proponents anticipate, there is a risk of a bumpy path ahead — and policymakers would do well to study the parallels from 26 years ago.

item.title: Warsh signals steady Fed outlook despite inflation jump
item.description:
Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh said Friday that the economy has largely performed as expected since September's rate hike, hinting that little has changed in the central bank's outlook.

Why it matters: The Fed is weighing another interest rate increase later this month as inflation heats up and the economy remains strong.

What they're saying: "Over the month or so that's transpired since then, the world has broadly conformed to our expectations," Warsh said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, referring to the Fed's September meeting.

  • Warsh, interviewed by IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva, offered no explicit signal about October: "I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year."
  • His remarks come just before the Fed's standard pre-meeting blackout period ahead of the Oct. 27-28 policy meeting.
  • "It's hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices," he said, alluding to conversations with international counterparts in Bangkok.

State of play: The Fed raised rates last month for the first time since 2023 to contain inflation fueled by the Iran war.

  • Minutes showed most officials expected another hike this year, though the timing remained unclear.
  • Vice chair Philip Jefferson, New York Fed president John Williams and governor Christopher Waller have signaled that the Fed could hold off in October, with Waller noting that rate hikes need not come at consecutive meetings.

Friction point: Fresh data this week showed inflation accelerated in September, with signs of price pressures extending beyond energy into services.

  • Odds of an October hike jumped to 50% from 22% after Wednesday's hotter-than-expected inflation report, before retreating to 28% Thursday afternoon, per CME FedWatch.

Between the lines: Warsh acknowledged that AI is boosting spending before its longer-term productivity benefits materialize, while investment beyond AI is also strengthening the economy.

  • Warsh said AI was contributing to a "massive investment surge" in the U.S., calling the investment boom "probably the most important thing that's happening in the global economy on the upside."
  • Warsh said AI could ultimately make economies more productive and generate greater wealth. But he said the AI transition was "likely to be a very bumpy one."

What to watch: Warsh announced that the Fed will hold the first field hearing of its productivity and jobs task force on Nov. 16 in the Bay Area, bringing together outside experts to examine how AI and other technologies are reshaping the economy.

  • The task force is one of five Warsh launched shortly after becoming Fed chairman to rethink how the central bank approaches monetary policy.

item.title: Geothermal finds rare political sweet spot amid AI boom
item.description:
Geothermal — power drawn from the Earth's natural heat — is pulling off something remarkable in today's hyperpolarized America: Winning fans across the political spectrum.

Why it matters: The bipartisan appeal, combined with surging electricity demand from AI, is helping fuel investment in a niche energy source yet to prove it can compete at scale.

Driving the news: Geothermal received unusually extensive attention in a bipartisan Senate bill introduced late last month to expedite infrastructure permitting.

  • The House this summer passed a package containing several of the same geothermal provisions, including measures sponsored by lawmakers as ideologically distant as Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Mike Kennedy (R-Utah).

The rising cachet of geothermal is the product of three trends converging:

  1. Technologies adapted from the oil and gas industry, including fracking, are making it possible to tap heat in more places than just far-flung hot springs and volcanoes.
  2. Tech companies, on the hunt for reliable electricity, are willing to pay a premium for next-generation geothermal to power data centers.
  3. Investment is surging as companies race to scale a renewable energy source that can generate power around the clock.

Catch up quick: The geothermal-specific provisions in the Senate bill go further than the broader permitting reforms offered to other renewable energy sources, including wind and solar.

  • The bill would make it easier for geothermal developers to explore and lease federal land, speed up drilling permits and exempt certain activities from environmental reviews.
  • Geothermal retained federal clean-energy tax credits in Republicans' sweeping tax law last year, even as wind and solar faced an accelerated phaseout.

State of play: Fervo Energy, an advanced geothermal company that went public earlier this year, is at the leading edge of this convergence. It was founded nearly a decade ago by Tim Latimer, a former drilling engineer in the oil and gas industry.

"I don't think any of us saw in 2017 that a few years later we would be in the biggest demand power boom for electricity that we had ever experienced," said Latimer during a recent on-stage interview with Axios in an event aptly titled "The energy source nobody argues about."

  • The AI boom has "accelerated our business tremendously."
Chart: Amy Harder/Axios; Note: Other includes project finance and debt. Fervo's IPO proceeds reflect capital raised at the time of its listing, not its current market value; Data: Currence

The intrigue: Geothermal's appeal crosses traditional political divisions precisely because it doesn't fit neatly into Washington's usual energy-policy boxes.

  • Its renewable characteristics appeal to Democrats.
  • Its reliance on drilling expertise and overlap with the oil and gas industry appeals to Republicans.
  • Its ability to provide stable, carbon-free electricity makes it attractive to utilities and tech companies.

By the numbers: The average winning bid for federal geothermal leases has surged, reflecting growing commercial interest.

  • The average winning bid in 2023 was $10 an acre, and so far this year, the average is $182, according to Guy Cohen, a geothermal analyst at the market intelligence firm Currence.
  • A record $1,207-an-acre bid was placed for a single parcel in Utah this summer.

Reality check: Geothermal's political popularity and investment boom are running ahead of its commercial reality. The technology remains expensive, and questions persist about whether it can reliably generate electricity over decades.

  • Geothermal currently generates less than 1% of U.S. electricity, and those eye-popping leases are for the right to explore for geothermal, not for active geothermal wells.
  • Fervo's stock has fallen nearly 70% from its first-day closing price following its IPO earlier this year, amid what Axios Pro calls a broader slowdown among energy startups.
  • Tom Erb, Fervo's government affairs and policy manager, says the construction costs at its flagship project in Utah are about half those of new nuclear plants. He acknowledged that underground heat can diminish over time, requiring additional drilling, but said those costs are factored into company projections.

What they're saying: Jigar Shah, a former Energy Department official under President Biden, says geothermal's current momentum still depends on state policies encouraging clean electricity and tech companies willing to pay a premium.

  • "I don't think this moment would work without above-market mandates from states or the data centers," Shah said.

Friction point: Geothermal has also encountered local opposition, particularly over water.

  • Traditional geothermal projects can disrupt hot springs and wetlands critical to wildlife, said Patrick Donnelly of the Center for Biological Diversity.
  • Newer technologies like Fervo's avoid some of those risks, he said, but questions remain about their water consumption.

What we're watching: Geothermal has found something rare in Washington: Political consensus. The test now is whether that consensus survives the industry's growth.

item.title: Banks are pulling back as AI's massive debt pile disconnects from economic reality
item.description:
Wall Street appears to be hitting its limit on AI, and financiers are starting to say the quiet part out loud: All of this AI spending doesn't look like it can pay off, at least not for everyone.

Why it matters: The gap between what it costs to build AI infrastructure and what companies are actually paying to use it is widening. Wall Street's anxiety is surging as the debt piling up to fund data centers and chips looks increasingly disconnected from economic reality.

Driving the news: A massive gap is opening up between AI infrastructure spending and expected returns.

  • While AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, research from Gartner forecasts they will generate no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over that same period.
  • More than $4 trillion in AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of write-downs by the end of 2032 if companies maintain their current investment pace.
  • Gartner also predicts that more than 80% of specialized AI cloud providers, known as neoclouds, will cease operating independently by 2030.

Case in point: CoreWeave, one of the largest neoclouds with among the closest ties to Nvidia — the AI boom's financial and spiritual foundation — has faced a multiday sell-off of its stock and debt.

  • Yields pushed above 15% and its stock tumbled 15.5% before rebounding after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang spoke up on the company's behalf.

Follow the money: Sources on Wall Street used to tell Axios that as long as the AI buildout was paid for in cash, there was nothing to worry about. But today, a third of the capex being spent on AI is coming from debt, and capital markets are showing signs of severe fatigue.

  • It's getting harder to secure financing. Global AI-related debt issuance plunged to $23 billion in September 2026, down sharply from $113 billion in June, per the Financial Times.
  • Banks are actively pulling back to avoid concentration risk, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon confirming his bank is tightening up on credit.
  • Infrastructure projects and providers are struggling: Approximately $18 billion in bank loans for an Oracle data center campus recently slid into stressed territory, while Nvidia-backed AI cloud provider Firmus shelved an IPO that sought a valuation north of $30 billion.

Zoom in: The constant spending relies on the belief that compute demand will never falter — a belief that has structural cracks.

  • Reflection AI co-founder Ioannis Antonoglou told Semafor that businesses may need "a decade or two decades" to fundamentally redesign their operations around AI.
  • That's 10 to 20 years of companies slowly adopting the technology that's being built (expensively) today.

Between the lines: This creates a mismatch: Data centers and chips require enormous investment today, but the returns that could justify that spend will take years to materialize.

  • Put bluntly, there is a massive gap between AI spending and AI revenue, one that won't close for many, many years.
  • At the same time, companies that are adopting AI quickly are getting smarter about using tools more efficiently, turning to open-weight models that are less compute-intensive to cut costs.

Reality check: Look at Anthropic's latest financials for a counterpoint to the bears.

  • The company is raking in cash, turning free cash flow positive in the third quarter and growing revenue nearly 50% compared to the April-to-June period.
  • But even Anthropic's staggering growth has slowed, albeit expectedly because trees can't grow to the sky.

The bottom line: The debt-fueled AI buildout is not an isolated problem for tech investors alone to worry about.

  • The stock market and economy have become increasingly tied up with the AI boom.
  • If the AI bet doesn't work, markets and the economy could falter as well.

item.title: Trump says Fort Hood shooter's execution will not be livestreamed
item.description:
President Trump said in a Thursday Truth Social post that the execution of the convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by firing squad will not be live-streamed.

The big picture: The president's post walks back an idea that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth pitched last week, setting off an avalanche of bipartisan condemnation.

Driving the news: "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump's post read.

  • He added, "That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose."
  • Trump noted that he thinks "streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die."
  • That seemingly included Vice President JD Vance, who said he wouldn't watch the execution.
  • House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) warned footage of the execution could become a "recruiting tool for future terrorists."

What they're saying: Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement provided to Axios that Trump and Secretary Hegseth discussed the decision ahead of the Truth Social post.

  • Parnell added: "The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned."

Catch up quick: The Pentagon previously confirmed that the December execution would be streamed after Hegseth said in an interview with Real America's Voice that it would be made "public."

  • But the plan received swift pushback from Republicans and Democrats in Congress alike, as well as from clergy and survivors of the horrific 2009 attack.
  • Even though most Americans support executing Hasan, a vast majority oppose livestreaming his death by firing squad, according to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll out Thursday.
  • Representatives for TikTok and Newsmax told Axios their platforms wouldn't allow execution livestreams or clips, Axios' Sara Fischer reported.

Friction point: The reversal also comes after Axios' Marc Caputo reported that the president himself was privately expressing doubts about the public execution after being deluged with a chorus of negative sentiment.

  • He was initially full-throated in his approval of the idea — but it took roughly a week for the plan to crumble.

Go deeper: Hegseth's public execution plan meets the age of viral violence

Editor's note: This story has been updated with a statement from the Pentagon.

item.title: "Mommy and daddy" play nice: Apple and Meta team up to bring open-source Muse to Macs
item.description:
Apple and Meta, whose leaders have spent years trading barbs over privacy and the future of computing, are joining forces to bring one of America's most powerful open-weight AI models to Apple's high-end Macs.

Why it matters: The collaboration marks a striking detente between two longtime Silicon Valley rivals, underscoring how the AI race is reshaping relationships across the technology industry.

  • The companies still compete over devices and the next generation of computing, but both see an opportunity in bringing powerful AI capabilities to personal computers.
  • "We're excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again," Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang told Axios.

Driving the news: Meta is releasing Muse Spark Open, a model similar to Muse Spark 1.3 that it says is the most powerful U.S.-developed open-weight AI model available.

  • Meta joins a host of Western AI companies that have released powerful open-weight systems that promise to slash AI costs, provide companies with more control and offer an alternative to the Chinese AI ecosystem.
  • Nvidia on Tuesday released updated versions of its Nemotron family of models, and U.S.-based Reflection AI and France's Mistral both released new open-source models last week.
  • As proof of Muse Spark Open's capabilities, Meta worked with Apple to make the model run locally across two or four connected Mac Studios powered by Apple's M5 Ultra chips, using Apple's MLX framework.

Zoom in: The prospect of a powerful model — it has 816 billion parameters — running on Apple hardware offers a proof of concept for how companies could build their own AI systems.

  • That could give companies more alternatives to Nvidia GPUs and proprietary models from leading AI companies, potentially shifting some of the economics of AI.
  • Meta's model will be free to download, with a license allowing commercial use, and will also be available through cloud providers and developer tools.

What they're saying: Wang said the companies have been working together for several months, with Daniel Gross, a former Apple executive now at Meta, helping bring the two sides together.

  • "I think he played a really big role in kind of getting the two companies to work nicely together," Wang said in a telephone interview.

Flashback: Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg have repeatedly clashed over privacy and their competing business models.

  • In 2018, amid Facebook's Cambridge Analytica scandal, Cook was asked what he would do if he were Zuckerberg. "I wouldn't be in this situation," Cook replied. Zuckerberg called Cook's comments "extremely glib."
  • The rivalry intensified in 2021, when Apple introduced new privacy protections that struck at the heart of Facebook's ad business. Zuckerberg reportedly told employees that Facebook needed to "inflict pain" on Apple over the dispute, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The big picture: The AI race is making for some strange bedfellows, scrambling long-standing Silicon Valley rivalries and even bringing together political adversaries.

  • Anthropic is leasing up to $15 billion per year of computing capacity from Elon Musk's SpaceX, even as it competes with his AI company.
  • Microsoft, OpenAI's longtime partner, is investing billions in rival Anthropic and incorporating its Claude models into its own products.
  • And in Washington, progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders and MAGA strategist Steve Bannon have found common ground in calling for tougher AI safeguards and challenging the power of Big Tech.

Between the lines: The Apple-Meta collaboration doesn't mean the companies have resolved their differences, but it suggests those disagreements no longer prevent them from working together when their interests align.

  • Meta benefits from making its AI models widely available, while Apple can showcase the capabilities of its most powerful computers.
  • And because the model runs locally, Meta doesn't receive users' prompts or other information — sidestepping the privacy concerns that have long divided the companies.

"Meta has no control or visibility to any of that," Wang said of how developers use the model.

Yes, but: Making powerful AI models openly available raises concerns that bad actors could remove safeguards and use the technology for cyberattacks or biological threats.

What we're watching: Whether the collaboration marks the beginning of a broader relationship between Apple and Meta.

  • For now, Apple is helping demonstrate that Meta's AI models can run locally on its computers. A more significant step would be Apple incorporating Meta's models into Apple Intelligence, giving the Facebook parent a role in powering Apple's own AI features.

The bottom line: Wang acknowledged that Apple and Meta will continue to compete in some areas, but said that doesn't have to prevent them from working together.

  • "Where it makes sense to collaborate and partner, we want to be able to do so," he said.

item.title: The too-hot-for-comfort economy
item.description:
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

Data this week has all told the same story: This is a rip-roaring U.S. economy with all the inflationary pressures that might imply.

The big picture: It puts Warsh and the Fed in a difficult jam. Top officials have signaled patience in further interest rate hikes in recent weeks, but the latest data implies broader inflationary pressures than previously thought, testing that conviction.

  • There is scant evidence that price pressures are receding on their own and growing reason to fear that they are becoming more entrenched, which could compel a more aggressive rate-hiking response.

Driving the news: On Thursday the government said the Producer Price Index rose 1.3% in September, the highest since 2022 and far above the 0.6% analysts expected. It came on the heels of a too-hot-for-comfort reading on consumer prices Wednesday.

  • Also Thursday, September retail sales notched a 0.8% rise, versus the 0.4% analysts had expected. And the August number was revised higher.
  • There were only 199,000 initial claims for unemployment benefits last week, remaining near historic lows.

Between the lines: The U.S. growth juggernaut shows no sign of diminishing — but neither do the price pressures that have bedeviled the economy for nearly five consecutive years.

  • If anything, the PPI and CPI data released this week suggest inflation is broadening, showing up in sectors well beyond energy.

State of play: In his appearance at the International Monetary Fund's meetings in Thailand Friday (11:30pm ET Thursday), Warsh has a final opportunity to comment before the Fed enters its customary quiet period in advance of a policy meeting that concludes Oct. 28.

  • Colleagues including New York Fed president John Williams and vice chair Philip Jefferson gave rather clear signaling in the last couple of weeks that they see little urgency to raise rates at a second consecutive meeting this month.
  • Warsh faces a dilemma. If he affirms that stance in spite of the hot price data, it could raise doubts about his determination to bring inflation under control.
  • If he seems inclined to raise rates, he could seem overly reactive to a couple of economic releases, contrary to his stated goal of making the Fed less "data-point dependent."

The intrigue: Surprisingly, bond yields are down Thursday despite the hot PPI number — and a surge in yields following the CPI number Wednesday mostly reversed later in the trading session.

  • It seems to reflect a flight to quality among traders as optimism around the AI buildout fades. With semiconductor and related stocks down, money looks to be flowing into safer Treasury securities.
  • The policy-sensitive two-year Treasury yield briefly touched 4.95% after the CPI number Wednesday, implying significant Fed rate hikes ahead. It was down to 4.72% Thursday morning — an astonishing move for any 24-hour period, let alone one that included hotter-than-expected inflation data.

What they're saying: "Today's September PPI report reinforces Wednesday's CPI message that inflation is turning higher and moving in the wrong direction for the Fed," Nationwide financial market economist Oren Klachkin wrote in a note.

  • "AI continues to lend upside pressure from categories directly and indirectly tied to the buildout. Businesses seem to be passing higher costs onto customers as the proxy for margins rose heftily in September."

item.title: CEO confidence drops into negative territory
item.description:
Data: The Conference Board and The Business Council; Chart: Axios/Emily Peck

CEO confidence in the U.S. economy sank into negative territory earlier this month, finds a survey out Thursday morning from the Conference Board.

Why it matters: Business leaders are mind-melding with most consumers, whose opinions on the economy are now lower than during the pandemic.

  • Such sour sentiment is shaping up as a key issue in the midterms just weeks away.

Where it stands: The CEO Confidence Index fell to 46 in the most recent period, down from 52 just three months ago — any number below 50 connotes negative sentiment.

  • The nonprofit Conference Board and the Business Council surveyed 131 Fortune 500 CEOs from Sept. 21-Oct. 5.
  • The survey measures how chief executives at major public companies feel about current economic conditions and their expectations for the economy and their own industries over the next six months.

By the numbers: 41% of CEOs expected economic conditions to worsen — up from 19% in the previous quarter.

  • Executives' concerns over cybersecurity, AI and geopolitics rose significantly from three months ago.
  • 94% of CEOs cited cybersecurity threats among their top AI-related concerns.

The surge in energy prices — particularly diesel, which is crucial to companies' energy costs — also contributed to the fall in sentiment, Dana Peterson, chief economist at the Conference Board, tells Axios.

  • "All these inflationary shocks, one after the the other, is weighing down on the confidence of both CEOs and consumers," she says.

Between the lines: The key worry when CEO moods darken is the spillover into the economy, as they pull back on spending and hiring.

Reality check: Despite their dimming views, CEOs have for the most part maintained their spending plans, per the survey.

Case in point: A separate survey also out Thursday morning found that 89% of U.S. CEOs said they expected to increase headcount over the next three years as AI creates more business opportunities.

  • "As we put more AI into our processes and platforms, the capacity opens up," Tim Walsh, the CEO of KPMG, which conducted the survey, told Axios' Nathan Bomey.
  • "What you're seeing there is CEOs being really optimistic that they can actually expand their business, which is going to result in a bigger workforce for them."

The bottom line: CEOs are gloomy about the economy, but their dark mood hasn't yet translated into a meaningful pullback in investment plans.

item.title: Anthropic brings Wall Street an AI bull case
item.description:
AI companies for years have promised that smarter models would be worth the staggering cost to build them. Anthropic on Wednesday made that case in cash.

  • The company presented eye-popping financials to investors, saying it was cash flow positive in the third quarter, with revenue surging nearly 50% to $16.8 billion compared with the April-to-June period.

Why it matters: As Wall Street broadly spent the day fearing an AI bubble, Anthropic offered what investors have been desperate to see: evidence that frontier AI can be a sustainable business.

State of play: The S&P 500 fell by more than 1% for the first time in 53 sessions, while Anthropic showed off a balance sheet that promises profitable AI, sources told Axios.

Zoom in: Consider just one of the stats reported by Anthropic: The company is cash flow positive even as some of the world's most profitable companies are struggling to keep their AI spending in check.

  • For context, Google parent Alphabet, long a money-printing machine, turned free cash flow negative in its second quarter as AI infrastructure investment soared.
  • Investing gurus — especially those focused on the frothiness of companies relative to their underlying value — have long seen free cash flow as a gold standard for the long-term health of a business.
  • Anthropic, a much younger company competing in the same expensive AI race, says it was cash flow positive in the third quarter. The Anthropic figures were first reported by the Financial Times.

Yes, but: The company's blistering pace of growth appeared to slow compared with the difference between the first and second quarters, when sales more than doubled.

  • Few investors saw growth as likely to continue at that pace, especially while the company faced ferocious competition from OpenAI.

Between the lines: Anthropic's latest financial disclosures reinforce what analysts and investors have been telling Axios:

  • The company's early bets on frontier intelligence and enterprise adoption are translating into meaningful financial gains that put it on track for the largest IPO in history. Some investors expect it to reach a $2 trillion valuation.

Flashback: Anthropic's early bets on coding expertise, business customers and spending discipline have paid off.

  • Claude Code, a viral hit that brought users to Anthropic in droves, reached an estimated annualized revenue of $6 billion to $7 billion by late summer, per Bloomberg Intelligence. Customers have generally been reluctant to switch once they've adopted it, per PitchBook data.
  • Anthropic charges roughly 20% to 30% more than competing models, according to Bloomberg Intelligence, a pricing power that BI's global head of tech research Mandeep Singh views as sticky given the level of intelligence customers get from Anthropic tools.
  • Anthropic's API business generates an estimated 90% of revenue using just 58% of the computing power needed to run its models, resulting in an estimated 92% gross margin before certain expenses, per SemiAnalysis.

Reality check: Anthropic hasn't solved every financial challenge associated with the AI buildout.

  • The company still faces enormous training costs and stock-based compensation expenses, which could weigh on its underlying profitability.
  • And Anthropic faces more than $500 billion in planned infrastructure and computing spending over the next decade.
  • Its premium pricing could also face pressure from increasingly capable, cheaper open-weight models.

What we're watching: Whether Anthropic can sustain its technological and financial advantages as it expands its frontier intelligence offerings into additional niche areas beyond coding.

  • The company's total addressable market will be a critical figure in its IPO paperwork.
  • One Anthropic investor said they're eager to see how the company thinks its leading-edge intelligence can translate into breakthroughs in drug discovery and other businesses beyond software.

The bottom line: Anthropic is showing Wall Street how frontier intelligence can turn into an actual business right when investors needed some good news.

item.title: Scoop: "OG" Bill Gates returns to wage war on AI risks
item.description:
Bill Gates is gearing up to dramatically expand his AI safety push, personally leaning on business leaders and considering a major deployment of his resources, sources tell Axios.

Why it matters: The formidable, sharp-elbowed Bill Gates who built Microsoft is back, and he's directing his competitive fire toward what he has come to see as one of the most important causes of his lifetime.

  • "I can reach CEOs on this better than you can," Gates told one person he consulted on AI safety, showing an eagerness for combat that associates say is a return to "OG" form.

Driving the news: Once a voice for optimism on AI, Gates has grown dismayed by an escalation of model capabilities, alarming security incidents and what he sees as insufficient regulation, sources say.

item.title: Scoop: The FTC demanded documents from AI giants over recent safety incidents
item.description:
The Federal Trade Commission on Wednesday sent civil subpoenas to AI giants seeking documents about safety incidents that have spiraled into an industry crisis.

  • The FTC sought documents from Anthropic and OpenAI in a probe focused on potential consumer protection violations, a person familiar told Axios.

Why it matters: The investigation is one of a number of steps the administration has taken to show a firm hand with AI companies after multiple incidents in which unreleased models hacked websites or took deceptive or aggressive steps in testing.

State of play: The agency on Wednesday sent out civil investigative demands, which help the government gather evidence and investigate ahead of potential litigation.

  • They are more than 50 pages long each and ask for documents concerning security incidents and safeguarding practices. The agency is also asking for marketing materials and documents detailing company privacy policies, the source said.
  • Investigative demands will be sent to third-party AI organizations at a later date, the person familiar said.

What they're saying: "As we improve our models and they increasingly help people in their day-to-day lives, safety remains a top priority," an OpenAI spokesperson said. "We will engage constructively with the FTC."

Zoom in: The FTC plans to compel top AI executives to testify about their products, according to the source.

  • The agency has investigative authority to examine actions related to consumer harms that could be seen as unfair or deceptive. Those can relate to a wide range of misbehavior, including how companies charge for services or if they're alleged to have misled users.
  • AI companies continue to face scrutiny about the safety of their products. FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson has echoed the view of other administration figures and executives that AI systems shouldn't be released if they aren't safe.
  • OpenAI faces a litany of lawsuits. A group of state attorneys general on Wednesday sued OpenAI under consumer protection laws for allegedly misleading users, including children, on the safety of its chatbot.

The big picture: The Trump administration has taken on a more aggressive posture toward AI companies as safety incident disclosures continue.

  • President Trump's newly minted Super Intelligence Force, which Ferguson co-chairs, last week responded to the "fraudulent" use of government systems by Anthropic's AI by announcing an industry-wide mandate to immediately notify and remediate when incidents occur.
  • The SI Force is set to meet on Thursday, sources familiar said.

item.title: AI tools are aiding would-be spies
item.description:
AI tools are now exacerbating a largely hidden problem that frontier AI companies have been contending with for years: the risk that employees will exploit their access to spy on their employers.

Why it matters: The same AI tools that companies are racing to release can also help people plan crimes and develop the technology to carry them out, creating another security headache for the companies building them.

Driving the news: Federal prosecutors charged Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national who has been an OpenAI engineer since July 2025, with allegedly attempting to intercept private conversations at OpenAI.

  • Around Sept. 30, the company found a "surreptitious audio recording device" that was plugged into a USB port in the back of a television in an executive conference room.
  • OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its own AI models to help "understand the device and where it had come from."

Zoom in: Investigators allege Alfozan used AI tools to research company meeting rooms and develop recording equipment, according to an FBI affidavit.

  • Alfozan used a "productivity agent" to ask basic information about OpenAI's offices, the documents say. Those queries included: "What meeting was this presented at and when was it record?," "List meeting rooms in (company) that are 6+", and "can you list today's meeting in this room."
  • Investigators also said that an AI chatbot account tied to his spouse asked the model to build a "continuous audio recorder" and to add "browser access an controls," as well as encrypt the memory card where the recordings were saved.
  • The complaint didn't say whether any sensitive conversations were successfully recorded.

The big picture: This is just the latest case where AI tools have helped people carry out alleged crimes.

  • Prosecutors say they discovered a Nebraska man's use of ChatGPT before a bank robbery, including asking the model for assistance with stripping and repairing a handgun. He was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison in August.
  • Last year, authorities said a man used ChatGPT to help plot the explosion of a Tesla Cybertruck outside of the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas.

Flashback: Alfozan's case has caught viral attention across news sites and social media, but it isn't the first time a tech employee has been arrested for allegedly stealing AI trade secrets.

  • In 2024, the Justice Department indicted ex-Google software engineer Linwei Ding for stealing AI technology secrets and sharing them with two Chinese companies.
  • Earlier this year, a federal jury found Ding guilty on several counts of economic espionage and theft of trade secrets.

Threat level: Now, AI tools are adding a new dimension to corporate espionage, potentially making it easier for less-sophisticated actors to build spying devices while giving investigators new ways to retrace their steps.

The bottom line: AI models are creating security headaches for companies not only when they break out of containment, but also when people use them to plan and carry out crimes — including espionage against their own internal workings.

item.title: New inflation warning sign
item.description:
America's inflation problem is becoming harder to contain, with new evidence Wednesday that price pressures are extending beyond the war-related energy shock rattling the global economy.

Why it matters: Inflation is squeezing household budgets and dimming hopes for relief. It is also increasing the prospect that the Fed will have to raise interest rates further.

What they're saying: "Higher energy costs are beginning to seep into broader services prices, increasing the risk that this inflation burst will persist," Fitch Ratings economist Olu Sonola wrote in a note.

  • The Consumer Price Index report "stands out as the first of the year in which price pressure appeared to be showing up in most corners of the consumption basket at once," Glenmede's Jason Pride wrote.

By the numbers: The CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, accelerating from August's 0.4% increase. The index increased 3.7% in the 12 months through September, compared with 3.4% in the prior month.

  • Gasoline prices surged 9% in September, accounting for more than half of the monthly jump in consumer prices.
  • Core prices, which exclude food and energy, advanced 0.3% for the second consecutive month. The annual rate accelerated to 2.6% from 2.4%.

The intrigue: Over the past three months, core CPI has risen at a 3.4% annualized rate, up notably from 2% in August — a sign that underlying inflation pressures are strengthening.

  • Inflation was stubborn in parts of the services economy that are less directly exposed to the energy price surge.
  • Shelter costs accelerated last month, rising 0.4%, while used car prices climbed 0.7%. Airfares jumped 1.2% as airlines grappled with soaring jet fuel costs.
  • "Supercore" — a narrower measure of inflation that excludes housing and energy services — was hot again last month. Prices in that category have risen at a nearly 4.6% annualized rate over the past three months.

The big picture: Top Fed officials in recent days have played down the urgency of another interest rate hike later this month. But Wednesday's inflation data swiftly revived bets that the central bank will have to act sooner than the following meeting, in December.

  • The two-year Treasury yield — particularly sensitive to Fed policy expectations — jumped roughly 12 basis points after the report.
  • Traders now see a 47% chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the Oct. 27–28 policy meeting, up from 22.1% yesterday (and 18% this time last week), according to CME FedWatch.

What to watch: Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg Tuesday that rising Treasury yields could help cool the economy, potentially reducing the need for another rate hike.

  • But the inflation report complicates that argument — showing that underlying price pressures remain stubbornly elevated.
  • Instead, the report lends support to more hawkish policymakers like Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who warned Monday that inflation was "relatively broad-based rather than concentrated in one component."
  • Hammack cited tariffs, the AI investment boom and rising services prices as additional sources of price pressures.

The bottom line: For American consumers, the risk is that another bout of inflation proves harder to shake — prolonging the affordability squeeze while keeping borrowing costs elevated.

  • The squeeze is already showing up in paychecks, with inflation outpacing wage growth for six consecutive months.
  • Real average hourly earnings fell 0.5% in September and were down 0.7% from a year earlier.

item.title: Social Security recipients will see rise in monthly payments next year
item.description:
Data: Social Security Administration; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

Social Security recipients will see the largest rise in their monthly payments in four years in January, with a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment.

Driving the news: The Social Security Administration announced the 2027 COLA adjustment for 76 million recipients of retirement and disability benefits, which by law is calculated based on the Consumer Price Index for the July-through-September quarter.

  • That will increase the average retiree's benefits by $900 a year, or $75 a month.
  • The agency also said that the cutoff for Social Security taxes will rise to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 this year. Income above that threshold is not subject to payroll tax.

How it works: The adjustment is, by statute, determined by the year-over-year change in CPI for the third quarter. Thus, the September data released this morning was the final input needed to calculate the adjustment.

Between the lines: The adjustment will mean more nominal income for seniors and disability recipients, amounting to a mild fiscal stimulus come January.

  • However, it also accelerates Social Security's looming fiscal problems, with its trust fund scheduled to expire in six years.
  • The most recent projections issued by the program's trustees assumed a 0.9 percentage point lower COLA for 2027, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget notes.

item.title: Inflation heats up as gas prices surge
item.description:
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

U.S. inflation picked up in September as soaring energy prices added to already stubborn price pressures, the Labor Department said on Wednesday.

Why it matters: The latest Consumer Price Index shows that the inflation fight is far from over — and makes further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes more likely as Americans struggle with higher costs.

By the numbers: CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, with the annual inflation rate at 3.7%, the government said.

  • That compares with a 0.4% monthly increase and a 3.4% annual rate in August.
  • Core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy costs, gained 0.3% on the month, compared with a similar monthly gain in August. In the 12 months through September, core CPI rose 2.6%, up from 2.4% the prior month.

Zoom in: The latest figures capture the toll of the Middle East war on American consumers as disruptions to global energy supplies push up fuel prices.

  • Gasoline prices spiked 9.1% in September after climbing 3.9% in August, when they accounted for more than a third of the monthly increase in consumer prices.
  • Prices for shelter, one of the largest components of the index, increased 0.4%, compared with a 0.3% gain in August.
  • Food prices were flat, compared with a slight 0.1% increase the previous month.

Zoom out: The surge in fuel prices has prompted extraordinary measures from the Trump administration, particularly as soaring diesel costs threaten to push up prices for goods transported across the country.

  • President Trump temporarily eased restrictions on tax-exempt diesel and lifted some U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel to boost global diesel supplies.
  • Airline fares surged 1.2% in September — bringing the annual increase to 22% — as higher jet fuel costs put pressure on ticket prices.

What to watch: The Social Security Administration is set to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for millions of retirees, based on inflation figures released on Wednesday.

  • The increase will take effect in January.

The big picture: The report comes as Federal Reserve officials weigh how soon to raise interest rates again, with policymakers divided over the persistence of inflation.

  • In a speech on Monday, Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack warned that inflation pressures extend well beyond energy — citing tariffs, AI investment and rising services prices.
  • Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg on Tuesday that higher Treasury yields are already helping restrain economic activity, possibly reducing the urgency of another rate hike this month.
  • New York Fed president John Williams said one more increase might be ahead this year, though he cautioned the central bank might not have to raise again in 2027.

The bottom line: In the wake of the inflation report, financial markets are now betting that an interest rate increase is more likely when the Fed meets later this month.

  • Odds of October rate hike jumped to 44% from 22% Tuesday, according to CME FedWatch data.
  • The yield on the two-year Treasury note — the security most reactive to Fed policy expectations — jumped 12 basis points, while the 10-year Treasury yield rose 7 basis points.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

item.title: Apple bets AI can finally make us want a smart home
item.description:
Apple's big new hardware bet for the AI era is here, and it's a ... smart display?

Why it matters: Cue the time machine and let's head back to 2014, when Amazon's Alexa shocked the tech world and led us to imagine a Jetsons-style home would be ours in the near future.

  • It wasn't, but Apple believes it could come soon. The iPhone maker is betting that modern AI can finally make good on that vision, unveiling a slew of new smart home devices Tuesday.

  • Apple's new products emphasize easy setup and integration with its existing ecosystem, while AI could help diagnose problems and coordinate devices.

item.title: AI's extreme heat challenge is moving from prediction to protection
item.description:
Cities and researchers are using AI to map and predict extreme heat risk, but new research suggests it's used far more to identify where people are in danger than to help officials respond.

Why it matters: As climate change intensifies extreme heat, better predictions won't protect vulnerable communities unless governments can turn them into action.

  • U.S. deaths associated with high temperatures rose 53% from an annual average of 2,670 in 2000–2009 to more than 4,000 in 2010–2020, according to a 2025 Yale study.

Driving the news: A study published in Climate Risk Management examined existing research on how AI and machine learning are being used to manage extreme heat.

  • Of the research papers reviewed, 98.4% focused on prediction and 59.2% on prevention. That's compared with just 10.4% on response, 3.2% on recovery and 1.6% on preparedness — a disparity the authors call a "research-to-implementation gap."
  • The research is heavily focused on using AI to forecast dangerous heat and identify who's at risk, with far less attention on how it can help officials decide what to do next.
  • "Where AI can actually add value is where prediction is central to the decision-making, and that's in scale or providing more granularity," said Karishma V. Patel, a RAND policy researcher who co-authored the study.

State of play: Turning sophisticated heat predictions into government action requires more than advanced models.

  • Cornell researcher Jennah Gosciak told Axios that having "robust data systems" that can ingest data from a variety of sources and then make it usable to practitioners "is most of the battle here."

Case in point: Google in June announced it had expanded its AI-powered Heat Resilience data from an initial 14-city pilot to more than 50 cities worldwide, giving urban planners building-level data to help target heat interventions.

  • The data uses AI and high-resolution imagery to map roof reflectivity down to individual buildings.
  • Google said data from the pilots helped inform decisions in several cities, including cool-roof ordinances and adaptation plans.

Reality check: Better information doesn't necessarily equal better outcomes.

  • Gosciak, who spent time as a Public Interest Technology Fellow with New York City Emergency Management, recently compared simpler heat-vulnerability indexes with more complex predictive algorithms for government heat decisions.
  • She described one important distinction as "slow versus fast data." Predictive algorithms may be more useful for time-sensitive decisions "tied to a specific trigger event," while simpler indexes can be better suited to longer-term planning.
  • One advantage of simpler indexes is that officials can explicitly choose which vulnerable populations to prioritize, added Gosciak, a Ph.D. student in Cornell's Information Science Department.

What's next: The next frontier may be less about making heat forecasts incrementally better and more about connecting predictions to interventions.

  • AI's value could lie in helping officials make "near real-time decisions" by integrating changing signals and providing "hyperlocal forecasting at granular levels," Patel said.
  • That could help officials respond to heat risks in real time and better understand compound threats involving heat, air pollution, wildfire smoke and drought, she said.

The bottom line: "What is important is not just that we can build AI-enabled technology, but it actually solves a problem or removes a bottleneck," Patel said.

item.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2 billion penalty over money laundering allegations
item.description:
The Treasury Department on Tuesday announced more than $1.2 billion in penalties against Bank of America for years of failures to report suspicious transactions and address shortcomings in its anti-money-laundering program.

Why it matters: The action includes the third-largest penalty in Treasury history.

What they're saying: "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a press release.

The big picture: The civil action comes less than a week after federal regulators fined American Express $350 million over similar failures to detect and report suspected money laundering.

Zoom in: Bank of America admitted to willfully violating federal anti-money-laundering laws — including requirements to maintain adequate safeguards and report suspicious transactions.

  • Regulators said the bank failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, resulting in more than $5 billion in suspicious activity that was either unreported or reported late.
  • More than $1 billion involved potential national security and other high-priority risks — including Chinese money-laundering networks and suspected trade-based money laundering linked to the U.S.-Mexico border, regulators said.

Of note: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency also assessed a $750 million civil penalty, the largest in the agency's history.

  • Treasury also announced an $11.6 million settlement with Bank of America over hundreds of apparent violations of U.S. sanctions, including those targeting Russia and Iran.

Flashback: Bank of America has been working to address deficiencies in its anti-money-laundering program since a December 2024 regulatory order. But regulators said significant problems persisted.

  • Officials said the bank prioritized revenue while limiting compliance resources — at times relying on law enforcement and other outside sources to identify suspicious activity.

The other side: In a statement, Bank of America said it has invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to fighting financial crime.

  • "Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators."

What to watch: Bank of America reports third-quarter earnings Wednesday. The bank said it will record a $1.2 billion, non-tax-deductible charge in those results.

  • The bank said costs associated with its ongoing efforts to fix compliance problems are already reflected in its expenses.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

item.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer
item.description:
Pope Leo has been diagnosed with lung cancer, the Vatican said Tuesday.

Why it matters: The Vatican disclosed the pontiff's health news just hours after he underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung.

What they're saying: "The surgery was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned, and the holy father has returned to his room," per a Holy See Press Office statement published Tuesday.

  • The office said in that statement it would provide more information shortly, and later followed up with news of Leo's diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, which they said tests "conducted beforehand" had led them to suspect.

Driving the news: The first American pontiff was admitted to Rome's Agostino Gemelli University Hospital on Tuesday afternoon for surgery.

  • "The Pope was in the operating room approximately three hours, while the operation itself lasted about 90 minutes. The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications," the statement said.
  • The Catholic Church leader carried out his usual duties Monday and was greeted by supporters and patients at the hospital, according to the Vatican statement.

Zoom in: Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer, per the Cancer Center.

  • It forms when the cells lining the outside of the lungs become cancerous. Its symptoms include persistent cough, shortness of breath and chest pain, amongst other things.
  • Patients with adenocarcinoma don't always experience symptoms early on, and it is often detected during a scan for a medical reason unrelated to lung cancer.

The big picture: Doctors discovered the nodule during routine medical checkups.

  • Leo said Sunday that the nodule "was detected at a very early stage and is well localized."
  • He thanked his supporters for their "spiritual closeness" and said he was entrusting himself to their prayers.

Go deeper: Pope Leo to have "nodule" removed from lung

item.title: Companies are building with AI — and exposing new security risks
item.description:
The amount of AI-related infrastructure exposed to the public internet jumped 63% in nine months, according to new Censys data shared first with Axios.

Why it matters: The AI boom isn't just creating new models and chatbots. It's creating a sprawling layer of software that companies will also need to inventory, patch and secure.

Threat level: Many of these tools connect AI applications to sensitive corporate data and other services, creating potential entry points for hackers looking to access company systems.

  • "It's a little bit beyond just like the tool itself, but these [tools] talk to some really sensitive systems," Emily Austin, a principal researcher at Censys and co-author of the report, told Axios.

The big picture: Censys identified nearly 268,000 internet-facing systems running 44 different AI-related products as of July, up from roughly 164,000 in October 2025.

  • These include the software used to connect AI models to databases, corporate applications and other services.

Between the lines: The ease of building and hosting AI applications is making it harder for companies to keep track of what software employees are using and whether it's secure.

  • Censys CEO Zakir Durumeric told Axios that companies were already struggling to keep track of their existing software even before employees started building their own AI applications.
  • These new AI apps can often connect to sensitive company information, such as emails, financial records and internal databases.

Zoom in: The most widely exposed product was n8n, a workflow automation platform that can connect AI agents to other applications and services.

  • Censys found nearly 114,000 internet-facing deployments of n8n, including roughly 77,000 running software versions affected by at least one recently disclosed critical vulnerability.
  • Researchers also found more than 54,000 exposed control panels for OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent that users can connect to personal accounts and other services.

Yes, but: The findings don't establish whether those deployments are actually vulnerable to exploitation, but they highlight the risks of exposing software that can access sensitive company systems.

The bottom line: Companies need to treat AI infrastructure like any other software they deploy, Austin said, including regularly reviewing, updating and securing the systems.

item.title: A golden age of corporate profits
item.description:
Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: After-tax profit data includes inventory and capital depreciation adjustments.

Corporate America is raking in record profits, luxuriating in luscious margins and capturing the largest chunk of the country's income on record.

Why it matters: The corporate bonanza is bolstering the stock market, but it may also be playing a role in the persistently sour sentiment among the American electorate.

The latest: Tuesday is the unofficial start of third-quarter earnings season as JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs and others report results.

Zoom in: Wall Street expects the members of the blue-chip S&P 500 index to continue to make it rain.

  • Third-quarter earnings per share are expected to grow roughly 29% for the index, compared with the quarter in 2025, according to estimate data collected by FactSet.
  • That's after a massive 50% annual increase in second-quarter earnings that was supercharged by the giant, non-operating gains on valuations of tech investments reported by Amazon and Alphabet. (Amazon, for example, penciled in its stake in Anthropic as boosting its profit by more than $50 billion.)
  • But even without those enormous gains, the numbers were quite strong, thanks to the AI boom that analysts expect to keep powering giant profits.

What they're saying: The market is still all about AI, but the gains are extremely concentrated.

  • "At the stock level, AI infrastructure stocks are expected to drive more than half of S&P 500 EPS growth in Q3," wrote Ben Snider, chief U.S. equity analyst with Goldman Sachs.
  • Snider noted that more than two-thirds of the total growth in S&P 500 earnings for the quarter is expected to come from just 10 stocks.
  • What's more, Micron Technology and Nvidia alone are expected to generate more than one-third of the growth in earnings for the blue chips, Snider wrote.

The big picture: Broader measures of U.S. corporate profitability captured by economic — rather than stock market — data also seem to show remarkable strength.

  • For the economy as a whole, after-tax corporate profits in Q2 jumped 18.2% compared with the same quarter of 2025.
  • And key measures of corporate profit margins across the entire U.S. economy are some of the fattest on record.
Data: FactSet, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: After-tax U.S. corporate profits, including inventory and capital consumption adjustments as a share of gross value added of U.S. corporate business. Reflects profits made within the U.S.; does not include profits produced overseas.

The other side: Boom times for corporate America have a flip side, however, with the so-called labor share of national income collapsing to some of the lowest levels on record.

  • The labor share tells you what percentage of the giant paycheck produced by the U.S. economy goes to workers in the form of wages and benefits, rather than to corporate profits, dividends, rents and interest paid to other economic actors, commonly summarized as "capital."

The bottom line: That decline helps explain the persistently sour mood of the American public toward the economy and its deep skepticism toward the AI boom that's producing this bonanza for American corporations.

item.title: Every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor as Microsoft reveals new Maia chip
item.description:
The trillion-dollar AI race is moving from software to silicon, as Microsoft's massive bet on its proprietary Maia chips proves Big Tech wants to wean itself off Nvidia's dominance.

Why it matters: Microsoft's plan to power its AI products with custom silicon shows how every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor, seeking lower costs, improved performance and more control.

  • The shift is particularly significant for inference — the computing needed to generate AI responses — as more sophisticated AI models and agents drive demand for computing power.

Driving the news: Microsoft unveiled Maia 300, its latest custom AI accelerator, saying it will begin deploying the chip in 2027 and it will become the primary inference system for its own products and services.

  • The company says Maia 300 will deliver 40% more AI tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems.
  • It's also designed to minimize unnecessary data movement between chips and memory, a growing bottleneck as AI models become more complex.

The big picture: Microsoft's plan is part of a much broader shift, with nearly all major AI players seeking Nvidia alternatives.

item.title: Two U.S. professors win Nobel prize in economics
item.description:
Stanford University's Robert E. Hall and Columbia University's Michael Woodford won the Nobel Prize in economics for research on how policymakers can stabilize economies, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Monday.

Why it matters: Their work helped shape how central banks set interest rates and communicate policy. The win comes as those institutions fight energy-driven inflation and risks to economic growth.

Zoom out: For decades, policymakers relied on economic models that linked higher inflation with lower unemployment. But that framework broke down during the 1970s stagflation when both prices and joblessness surged at the same time.

  • "The solution by Robert Hall and Michael Woodford was to build a new framework ground up," Timo Boppart, a member of the Nobel economics prize committee, said on Monday.

What they're saying: Woodford, who called into Monday's press conference hosted by the committee, said he was "elated" by the win.

  • "It's a tremendous honor. It's a surprise — but I'm feeling very good about it," Woodford said.

The intrigue: Asked by a reporter about the threat to the global economy, Woodford said the Middle East conflict has disrupted energy markets and driven price changes with consequences far beyond the region.

  • He pointed to the 2008 financial crisis as a key test of his research, when central banks cut interest rates to near zero but struggled to revive economic activity.
  • His framework helped explain how other tools, including forward guidance and asset purchases, could support the economy.

Zoom in: In research culminating in a landmark 2003 book, Woodford developed a framework linking businesses' pricing decisions to inflation and monetary policy.

  • Hall — a Stanford professor who chaired the committee that dates U.S. recessions for 46 years — showed in a 1978 paper how consumers' spending decisions reflect expectations about future income.

Of note: The prize comes with an award of 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), up from 11 million kronor last year, to be divided between the two winners.

Flashback: Recent economics Nobels have recognized research on technological progress, economic prosperity and labor markets.

  • Last year's prize went to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for their work explaining how innovation drives economic growth.
  • In 2024, Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson won for their research on how institutions shape economic prosperity.
  • Harvard economist Claudia Goldin won in 2023 for research that advanced the world's understanding of women's labor market outcomes.

item.title: Silicon Valley's horror shows
item.description:
Hollywood's hottest villain right now is the tech billionaire.

  • Four films hitting theaters this fall put some of Silicon Valley's most powerful and controversial figures in the spotlight: Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and Elizabeth Holmes.

Why it matters: Hollywood's portrayal of Silicon Valley and its leaders is getting darker as negative headlines about the tech industry seep into pop culture.

  • Once portrayed as brilliant but flawed innovators, tech leaders are increasingly being cast as creepy villains whose ambitions may do more harm than good.

Zoom in: This fall's tech billionaire films span genres, from documentaries to thrillers.

  • 💻 "The Social Reckoning," Aaron Sorkin's follow-up to his 2010 hit, "The Social Network," opened Friday with Jeremy Strong portraying a more sinister Mark Zuckerberg during the 2021 Facebook whistleblower leak. Sorkin takes some cinematic liberties with chronology and other details.
  • 🚀 "Musk," the four-hour documentary (including a 10-minute intermission) about Elon Musk's rise, is playing in select theaters and opens nationwide on Friday. The roller-coaster rollout of the film, directed by Oscar-winning documentarian Alex Gibney, included critical acclaim at the Venice Film Festival and legal threats from Musk's team.
  • 🩸 "You Can See Everything," out Friday, is an experimental documentary from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim that follows ex-Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before she went to prison. The studio, A24, says an "intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss." (More on the film.)
  • 🤖 "Artificial," a drama directed by Luca Guadagnino, stars Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and hits theaters Christmas Day. In the film, "[Garfield] depicts Altman as a manipulative, power-hungry psychopath who lies as easily as he breathes and will use anyone, anytime, anywhere to get what he wants," The Verge reports. The studio, NEON, calls it "the story of OpenAI and a two-decade artificial intelligence arms race. ... As the technology becomes more powerful and more valuable than anyone ever imagined, a battle rages over who should control the tech that could change the fate of humanity."

These projects represent a sharp turn away from some earlier movies and documentaries about Silicon Valley, like "Jobs" and "Something Ventured," which celebrated the ingenuity of founders and venture capitalists.

  • "With tech, it was an ardent love affair," says Margaret O'Mara, a University of Washington historian who studies Silicon Valley. "And when you fall out of love, you fall out of love fast."
  • "Our popular understanding of Silicon Valley and the products it makes has changed drastically."

Zoom out: Hollywood is reflecting the public's growing disillusionment with the tech industry.

  • Polls show Americans of all ages are quickly souring on AI and think it's moving too fast. Two in three Americans say social media has been bad for democracy, per Pew Research Center polling.
  • "Popular movies hold up a mirror to current social anxieties," says writer and editor-in-chief of Film Quarterly J.M. Tyree. Right now, "people are thinking about power consolidating in the hands of the few at the expense of the many."

The intrigue: Tech founders are compelling on-screen villains, Tyree says.

  • They bring together two archetypes: the ruthless businessman who's corrupted by greed, as seen in movies like "Citizen Kane" and "The Wolf of Wall Street," and the mad scientist who's morally ambiguous and employs science and technology recklessly, like in "Metropolis" or "Frankenstein."
  • Plus, their eccentricities make for good entertainment.

The bottom line: O'Mara, the Silicon Valley historian, notes: "One thing I have learned from studying the history of rich people is that extreme wealth makes you weird."

item.title: Pope Leo to have "nodule" removed from lung
item.description:
Pope Leo said Sunday tests had discovered a nodule in his lung, which he will have removed surgically this week.

The big picture: The first American pontiff, aged 71, is less than 18 months into a papacy that has been defined by public stances at odds with the White House, including clashes over immigration and deep skepticism about AI.

What he's saying: "Dear friends, during some recent medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is well localized. The doctors believe surgery is appropriate," the pope said during public remarks, per a translation from the Vatican.

  • "Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it. The operation is already scheduled for the coming days. I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers."

The pope did not explicitly say the nodule was malignant.

  • Vatican officials later said the operation would be in the next few days and the recovery would take about a week.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: As youth sports booms, churches compete for American families' Sundays
item.description:
America's youth sports boom is quietly rewriting Sunday mornings, turning the family calendar into a competition between the pews and the playing fields.

Why it matters: For generations, churches helped organize American family life around a shared weekly ritual. Youth sports are increasingly filling that role on Sundays — reshaping what families treat as sacred time.

  • The U.S. has undergone one of its fastest religious shifts in modern history, marked by a rapid increase in the religiously unaffiliated and in church closures. Youth sports are one of the less visible forces driving that broader cultural change.
  • As it's boomed into a multi-billion-dollar industry, more games are moving to Sundays, something less common a generation ago.
  • "The idea of missing church for sports is just assumed," Linda Flanagan, author of "Take Back the Game: How Money and Mania Are Ruining Kids' Sports — and Why It Matters," tells Axios. "It's just not even a consideration anymore."

By the numbers: Among parents of children ages 5-17, Sunday religious participation fell from 26.8% in 2003-07 to 16.7% in 2021-24, an Axios analysis of American Time Use Survey data found.

  • Meanwhile, youth sports participation climbed to 58% in 2024, up from 53.8% in 2022 and marking a third consecutive annual increase, according to the Aspen Institute's Project Play.
  • Another measure found 65% tried a sport at least once — the highest share in Sports & Fitness Industry Association data dating to at least 2012, the Aspen Institute's Project Play found.

State of play: The youth-sports industrial complex is rapidly commercializing, fueled by private equity, massive tournament complexes and the normalization of out-of-state travel teams.

  • Parents are increasingly treating sports not just as recreation, but as a primary identity and community anchor.

How it works: Youth sports often start in local rec leagues, then move into club and travel teams that play weekend tournaments across a wider region.

  • Across basketball, baseball, softball, volleyball and soccer, many weekend tournaments use Saturday for pool or preliminary play and Sunday for elimination rounds and championships.
  • That fuels cities' and towns' investments in sports complexes built to draw traveling families and their hotel and restaurant spending.

Zoom in: The average sports parent spends 3 hours, 23 minutes every day their child has a practice or game, including driving, attending activities, washing uniforms, preparing meals and communicating with coaches.

  • Families are spending heavily, too: The average sports family spent an average of $1,016 on a child's primary sport in 2024, up 46% from 2019, Aspen found.

What they're saying: Tim Morey, lead pastor at Life Covenant Church in Torrance, Calif., tells Axios that sports don't necessarily sever families from church, but they make attendance "more spotty" at times.

  • "If we inadvertently teach our kids that sports (are) more important than weekly worship, then everything is more important than weekly worship."

Yes, but: Religious institutions are attempting to adapt rather than surrender.

  • Morey said some families "divide and conquer," sending one parent to church and the other to the field.
  • Others have kids attend the first 10 minutes of service in their sports uniforms or stream services live from team hotels.

Between the lines: Youth sports can create the same sense of community that mirrors what church did — to a point, Flanagan said.

  • Parents form tight bonds because they spend so much time together, but competition for positions and playing time can also strain those relationships, Flanagan said.

The bottom line: For generations, Sunday was about getting the family closer to heaven.

  • For many families today, Sunday can also be about getting a daughter closer to UCLA's softball team.
